title: Orientation-selective microwave heating of laser-graphitized diamond at 2.45 GHz
authors: Massimiliano Zamengo, Meguya Ryu, Haoran Mu, Hsin-Hui Huang, Nguyen Hoai An Le, Tomas Katkus, Darius Gailevičius, Junko Morikawa, Saulius Juodkazis
abstract: Pristine diamond couples negligibly to a 2.45 GHz field. We show that femtosecond-laser inscription of a buried graphitic (sp2) architecture makes a 4 x 4 x 2 mm^3 N-doped (100 ppm) high-pressure high- temperature (HPHT) crystal absorb strongly, and that the absorption is switched by the orientation of the inscribed structure relative to the cavity electric field. With the 1.8 mm depth of a concentric grating along E, stepped power gave a smooth staircase to an indicated ~500C at 80 W followed, at 90 W, by an abrupt excursion to an indicated ~900C with surface roughening and terraced oxidation. Rotating the same sample so that the grating diameter lay along E, and an unmodified crystal in either orientation, gave no signal above the ~40C floor. We account for this by the depolarisation factors L of the sub-wavelength tracks, collapsed into one screening parameter S = Lσ/(ωε0εh), here, σ conductivity, ω - cyclic frequency, εh,0 - permittivity of host and vacuum, respectively. The model turns element length, diameter and writing regime into design variables for microwave absorption in a transparent host.
summary: This work demonstrates that by using femtosecond lasers to write graphitic structures into bulk diamond, one can create a material that strongly absorbs microwave energy at 2.45 GHz. Crucially, this absorption is highly dependent on the orientation of the written structure relative to the microwave electric field, enabling precise, tunable microwave engineering in transparent solids.
main_problem: The study investigates how laser-inscribed graphitic structures in diamond can be used to achieve highly controllable and orientation-selective microwave absorption and heating at 2.45 GHz.
main_result: Strong microwave absorption and subsequent high-temperature heating are only observed when the inscribed structure's depth axis is aligned perpendicular to the cavity electric field, demonstrating strong anisotropy.
method: The research combines femtosecond laser inscription to create conductive $	ext{sp}^2$ architectures in bulk diamond, followed by microwave heating measurements in a resonant cavity.
model_or_system: The system is an N-doped HPHT diamond crystal modified by laser-written graphitic gratings. The physics is modeled using effective loss factors ($\varepsilon''_{	ext{eff}}$) incorporating both dipolar and Ohmic dissipation, with orientation dependence parameterized by a screening factor $S$.
key_observables: Microwave absorption (measured via $T, R, A$), radiative temperature, resonant frequency ($\Delta f$), and quality factor ($Q$).
important_parameters: Microwave frequency (2.45 GHz), laser wavelength (1030 nm), structure depth ($\sim 1.8 	ext{ mm}$), and input power ($P_{	ext{in}}$ up to $100 	ext{ W}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on modeling the interface as a metal-semiconductor contact and assumes the validity of radiative pyrometry, while acknowledging the difficulty in separating temperature change from emissivity change.
figures_summary: Figures show the laser inscription geometry, the microwave cavity setup, temperature evolution during heating (showing plateaus and abrupt jumps), and spectral mapping of graphitic features.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the fundamental lack of absorption in pristine diamond to demonstrating strong, orientation-dependent absorption using laser-written structures. It details the thermal response under varying power and concludes with theoretical modeling of the absorption mechanism.
why_interesting: The precise control over microwave absorption via structural engineering (laser writing) in a transparent host material like diamond is highly relevant for developing novel quantum microwave components or sensing platforms.

Figure 3(b) shows the cavity resonance tracked simultaneously. The resonant frequency rises monotonically through the stepped ramp, by ∆f ≈1.7 MHz in total, mirroring the temperature staircase step for step, and then reverses at the onset of the abrupt excursion. The reversal coincides with the rise in reflected power. Frequency alone carries mainly reactive information — it responds to the sample permittivity and conductivity, but equally to thermal expansion of the cavity, displacement of the sample or its support, changes in coupling through the tuner, and oxidation-induced changes of sample geometry — while loss information resides in Q, which was not recorded synchronously.
